title: What everyone gets WRONG about Range of Motion
summary: A lecture on range of motion within technique (load, ROM, tempo). NH argues there is no universally optimal ROM; ROM only matters together with load and biomechanics, so the target is 'effective ROM', the part of the movement that puts the target muscle under the most stress. He criticises dogmatic full-ROM and lockout obsession (often rooted in powerlifting and weightlifting rules) and shows how trimming useless ROM on pullovers, lateral raises and RDLs improves load, reps and stimulus-to-fatigue, with tempo applied last.
claims: Training is a battle needing strategy (the program: volume, intensity, frequency) and technique (execution); both must be under control
Volume, intensity and frequency are the most important program variables for natural lifters and are equally important
Technique breaks down into load, range of motion and tempo; tempo is the least important of the three
Load is well understood: anything from about 60-100% of 1RM (he says 65-95%) across a wide rep range builds muscle
There is no universally optimal ROM: limb lengths differ, so travel distance and ideal ROM differ per person
ROM is the distance the lever travels against load, stretching or contracting the muscle; more ROM only helps if the load is heavy enough to challenge the muscle through it
Cutting ROM to add weight usually removes the part of the lift that stresses the muscle most, which is ego lifting
If your shallower squat allows more than about 20% more load than a below-parallel squat, you have cut too much ROM
Let ROM dictate the load, never the load dictate the ROM
ROM debates are often emotional and dogmatic ('it doesn't count'); people who take pride in their ROM while lifting far less are often coping
Serious lifters cut the bottom of the RDL to shift emphasis from glutes and lower back to hamstrings, and nobody calls that cheating
The lockout on bench and overhead press contributes little to chest and shoulder growth; lockout obsession comes from powerlifting and Olympic lifting rules where locking the elbow is required
Triceps work hardest early in the press when the elbow is most flexed, not at lockout
Insisting on lockout can cost reps in the range that matters most for the target muscle
'Joints are meant to lock' is an appeal to nature: humans lock knees to stand still, and all muscle work happens while joints are unlocked
The squeeze at the top isn't what builds muscle; travel distance under load does, though a squeeze may help feel the muscle
Many overhead pressers fight for the useless lockout yet skip the bottom portion where shoulder flexion and delt activation are greatest
Lock out if it keeps you in the groove and gets more reps with better load; never locking out to 'keep tension' can reduce total tension if it costs reps and load
Two valid reasons to limit ROM: it recruits the target muscle more, or it also makes you more performant (better tempo, load, reps)
Effective ROM is the portion of the ROM where the target muscle is under the most stress; lifters already pick standard lifts (45 lb plates on deadlifts, straight bar on bench) for effective ROM
A good partial should let you do more reps with more weight for the target muscle
Only about 30% of the pullover's ROM is effective; trimming the dead top and overextended bottom makes it 70-80% effective
Managing effective ROM also manages the stimulus-to-fatigue ratio; always chasing full ROM accumulates unnecessary fatigue
Lateral raises are best done in a range that stops before the top (and arguably short of the bottom); raising overhead disengages the delts, shifts work to the back and forces a lighter load
Only once ROM and load are set should you add tempo such as a slow negative through the effective range; starting with a fixed tempo hurts load and ROM
exercises: stop short of the full bottom
keeps hamstrings as target, less glute and lower back
prioritise the bottom range, lockout optional
shoulder flexion is greatest low in the lift
lock out only if it helps groove and reps
skip the dead top and overextended bottom; work the arc around the head
stop short of the top, possibly short of full bottom
keeps delts loaded, more load and reps
